author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Spare Key
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
Neri offered me the key in a velvet pouch.

That was how I knew something was wrong.

Neri was the kind of person who wrapped fragile archive seals in plain paper and put their own lunch in a tin that had lost its lid. Velvet meant ceremony, and ceremony usually meant somebody was trying to make a decision look less like a decision.

"What's that?" I asked.

"A spare key to the lower records cabinet."

"Why do you want me to have it?"

"Because you ask good questions."

I waited.

"And because," Neri continued, "the maintenance records may be important to understanding the second bell. If I am unavailable, someone should be able to open the cabinet."

The cabinet stood in Moonroot Archive, beneath a narrow window that let in just enough light to reveal the dust on its handles. Inside were copies of the old service-route plans, private correspondence whose release had not been authorized, and the burned ledger with the scratched-out signature.

I looked at the pouch.

"Who else has a key?"

Neri blinked.

"Me."

"Who knows you're giving me one?"

They hesitated.

That answered the question.

I set the pouch down on the table.

"I can't take it like this."

Neri looked hurt.

"I trust you."

"I know. I'm grateful. But trust isn't the same as authority."

Severus was cataloging a collection in the next room. He didn't turn around, though I could tell by the way his pen stopped that he'd heard every word.

Neri folded their hands.

"Someone has to be able to open the cabinet in an emergency."

"Then we need an emergency procedure. Not a secret transfer of a key to somebody you like."

They looked toward the window.

"I thought it would be simpler."

"It would be simpler for us. Not for the people whose records are in there."

I heard footsteps behind me.

Severus appeared in the doorway.

"An inconvenient distinction," he said.

Neri sighed.

"You two are impossible."

"Correct," Severus replied.

We brought the question to the archive committee. The meeting took place in the same room where Severus's private letters had once been opened without permission. The memory made everyone careful, which was one good use of discomfort.

The committee chair, Vale, argued that the cabinet should have two keyholders.

"Two isn't an accountability system," I said. "It's a number."

Tamsin, invited because the old service records contained structural plans, drew a diagram of the cabinet's contents and the reasons somebody might need access. Public maintenance documents could be copied and held openly. Private correspondence required separate handling. Emergency structural records needed a process that did not depend on Neri being awake.

Fen added a note about flood conditions.

"If water is rising," they said, "we can't wait for an argument about who has the right to read a tide chart."

We separated the records into categories. The tide charts and structural inspection drawings would be accessible to the emergency team with a logged sign-out. Private letters would remain sealed unless their recipients authorized inspection or a narrowly documented immediate danger justified it.

The burned ledger would remain available to the evidence team under supervision. Nobody could scrape it further in pursuit of a satisfying name.

Then we designed the key record.

It was a simple page: the date, the person opening the cabinet, the specific reason, which documents were accessed, whether copies were made, and when everything was returned.

No romantic histories. No traveler destinations. No list of who had looked worried when somebody arrived.

Maui came to the meeting late, carrying a basket of bread from Mara.

He looked at the diagram.

"Can we put two locks on it?" he asked.

Danse, who had come for the structural records, looked up.

"That might increase security."

Edda cleared her throat.

"Or make it harder for someone who can't reach the top latch."

Danse winced.

Maui put the bread down.

"Right. Not that."

I laughed.

After three hours, the committee approved a revised process. Neri would continue as archive steward. Severus would supervise evidence handling in his assigned hours. Tamsin and Fen could request emergency structural access using the public log. A second key would be kept in a sealed case in an accessible location, with a tamper-evident record.

I wasn't made keeper of anything.

I felt relieved.

When the meeting ended, Neri waited by the door.

"I thought you were the right person," they said.

"To hold the key?"

"To carry the responsibility."

I looked at the pouch, still on the table.

"Maybe I can help without owning the decision."

Neri smiled.

"You already did."

Outside, the rain had started again. The old stone under Lanternwell Square smelled cool and mineral, and water ran down the channels toward Tideglass.

Maui walked beside me.

"Do you ever wish somebody would just give you a mysterious key and tell you you're chosen?"

I looked at him.

"Sometimes."

He grinned.

"I could make you one."

"Please don't."

"Golden? With a jewel?"

"Absolutely not."

"Three jewels?"

I laughed.

He took my hand.

We passed the northern arch, where the departure notice had been updated. Then we stopped at the fountain to watch Neri's team install the new public sign-out board.

The process wasn't perfect. Somebody would forget a signature someday. An emergency could still force a difficult judgment. But at least everyone would know what the key opened and who was answerable for using it.

Maui looked toward the water.

"There's still a key you wear," he said.

I touched the brass shape at my neck, the one that fit the old maintenance hatches.

"Yes."

"Do you think it means you should open them?"

"No. I think it means I can help when the people affected have made a safe plan."

He nodded.

"That isn't much of a legend."

"It'll have to do."

He leaned close enough to kiss my forehead.

"Maybe the best legends are the ones where nobody gets trapped."

I smiled.

"Write that down before you forget it."

He pulled a scrap of paper from his pocket and did, in enormous letters that took up half the page.

Later, at home, we hung the scrap beside the tide chart.

It was a terrible piece of calligraphy.

It was a very good rule.
